notes: **Statement:** Equal volumes of all gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain an equal number of molecules (or moles). V ∝ n (at constant T and P). This fundamental law establishes the relationship between gas volume and particle count.
**Formulated by:** Amedeo Avogadro in 1811. He proposed that elemental gases like O₂, H₂, N₂ exist as diatomic molecules, resolving inconsistencies in Gay-Lussac's observations.
**Avogadro's Number (N_A):** 6.022 × 10²³ particles/mol. This precise value represents the number of atoms in exactly 12 grams of Carbon-12 and defines the mole as an SI base unit.
**Molar Volume:** At STP (Standard Temperature and Pressure: 0°C/273.15 K, 1 atm/101.325 kPa), one mole of any ideal gas occupies exactly 22.414 L (commonly rounded to 22.4 L).
**Historical Context:** Avogadro's hypothesis was largely ignored for 50 years until Cannizzaro championed it at the 1860 Karlsruhe Congress, establishing atomic weights and molecular formulas.
**Key Insight:** Avogadro distinguished between atoms (elementary particles) and molecules (groups of atoms), resolving Dalton's confusion about gas volumes in reactions.
**Example:** 1 mol H₂ (2.016 g) and 1 mol O₂ (32.00 g) both occupy 22.4 L at STP, demonstrating that volume depends on particle count, not mass.
**Application — Gas Stoichiometry:** In H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g), the volume ratio 1:1:2 directly reflects the mole ratio from Avogadro's law.
**Significance:** This law bridges the macroscopic world (measurable volumes) and the microscopic world (molecular quantities), forming the foundation of the mole concept and gas calculations.
confusion: ❌ 'Avogadro's number is 6.022 × 10²³ for all substances.' ✅ Avogadro's number is the number of particles in ONE MOLE of any substance — the number is always the same, but the mass of one mole varies.
❌ 'Equal volumes of gases always contain equal numbers of molecules.' ✅ Only at the same temperature and pressure. If T or P differ, the volumes differ.
❌ 'The molar volume is always 22.4 L.' ✅ Only at STP (0°C, 1 atm). At other conditions, use PV = nRT.
❌ 'Avogadro's law applies to solids and liquids.' ✅ It applies only to gases — the intermolecular distances in solids and liquids are too variable.
❌ 'Avogadro's law was accepted immediately.' ✅ It was largely ignored for 50 years until Cannizzaro championed it in 1860.
